1.title: Multi-Container Pod Patterns
1.text: Welcome to Module three: Multi-Container Pod Patterns. It covers the exam area Application Design and Build. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, and every task was run on a real cluster, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Why more than one container in a Pod. Init containers. Sidecars and shared volumes. Native sidecar containers. How to choose. Practice with five hands-on labs worth thirty-one points.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: Application Design and Build (twenty percent). Practice in this module: five labs, thirty-one points, about thirty-five minutes. Exam format: performance-based tasks in a live terminal, scored on the final cluster state. Validated on: Kubernetes version one point thirty-seven point zero.

1.title: Why more than one container in a Pod
1.text: Why more than one container in a Pod. The figure shows this: Containers of one Pod share the network and volumes. Exam tip: All containers of a Pod share the network and the mounted volumes, but not the image file system.

1.title: Why more than one container in a Pod, continued
1.text: Why more than one container in a Pod. All containers of a Pod run on the same node and share two things: the network (one I P address, local host reaches the other containers) and the volumes you mount into them. They do not share the file system of the image or the process list by default. Put two containers in one Pod only when they must work as one unit and be scheduled, scaled and restarted together.

1.title: Why more than one container in a Pod, continued
1.text: Why more than one container in a Pod. Init container. What the extra container does: runs to completion before the main containers start. Example: wait for a Service, download a file, set permissions. Sidecar. What the extra container does: runs next to the main container for its whole life. Example: ship logs, refresh a certificate, sync content. Ambassador. What the extra container does: a proxy that the main container talks to on local host. Example: connect to a database, hiding sharding or credentials. Adapter. What the extra container does: converts the main container's output to another format. Example: turn app metrics into the format a monitoring system reads. Ambassador and adapter are designs, not special Kubernetes fields: both are ordinary extra containers in spec dot containers.

1.title: Init containers
1.text: Init containers. spec dot init containers run one after another, each to completion, before the main containers start. If one fails, the kubelet restarts it (with restart Policy Always or On Failure ) and the main containers do not start. The Pod shows Init zero slash one, Init one slash two, Init Error or Init crash loop back off until they finish. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study. Exam tip: A Pod stuck in Init zero slash one: read the init container log with kube control logs pod dash c init container.

1.title: Init containers, continued
1.text: Init containers. They can use a different image from the app (tools the app image does not have). They share volumes with the main containers: an init container writes a file to an empty dir, the app reads it. Their resources count differently: the Pod's effective request is the larger of the biggest init container and the sum of the app containers. A Pod stuck in Init zero slash one: read the init container's log, kube control logs pod dash c init name, and kube control describe pod.

1.title: Sidecars and shared volumes
1.text: Sidecars and shared volumes. The classic sidecar shares an empty dir with the main container. The app writes a log file, the sidecar reads it. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study. Exam tip: You cannot add a container to a running Pod: recreate the Pod, or edit the Deployment.

1.title: Sidecars and shared volumes, continued
1.text: Sidecars and shared volumes. kube control logs weblog dash c tailer reads one container; with several containers you must give dash c, or use the all containers flag. kube control exec -it weblog dash c app then the command sh enters one. A Pod's containers cannot be added to a running Pod: edit the manifest and recreate ( k replace the force flag dash f ). Shared network. Containers in a Pod listen on the same ports: two containers that both bind port eighty clash. The other containers reach a web server in the Pod at H T T P colon slash slash local host eighty.

1.title: Native sidecar containers
1.text: Native sidecar containers. A sidecar declared as a normal container has two problems: it may start after the main container, and in a Job it never stops, so the Job never completes. Kubernetes solves this with native sidecars: put the sidecar in init containers and set restart Policy Always on that one container. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study. Exam tip: A native sidecar is an init container with restart Policy Always; it lets a Job complete.

1.title: Native sidecar containers, continued
1.text: Native sidecar containers. Starts. Init container: before the main containers, in order. Native sidecar: before the main containers, in order. Regular container: with the main containers. Keeps running. Init container: no, must finish. Native sidecar: yes, restarted if it exits. Regular container: yes. Stopped when the main containers end. Init container: n or a. Native sidecar: yes, after them. Regular container: n or a. Blocks a Job from completing. Init container: no. Native sidecar: no. Regular container: yes. A native sidecar can have its own probes (a startup probe tells the kubelet when the sidecar is ready, so the main container starts after it).

1.title: How to choose
1.text: How to choose. It must finish before the app starts: init container. It runs for the app's whole life and shares files or the network: sidecar (a native sidecar in a Job). The app should talk to a local proxy: ambassador. Output must change format for a consumer: adapter. It could run and scale alone: a separate Pod or Deployment, not the same Pod.

1.title: How to choose, continued
1.text: How to choose. Exam tip. In a task that says "add a container to the Pod", the Pod must be recreated: kube control get pod x dash o yaml x dot yaml, edit, k replace the force flag dash f x dot yaml. In a Deployment you can edit in place ( kube control edit deployment ), and the Pods are replaced for you. Exam tip. Init container problems show in the Pod status first: Init zero slash one. Always read kube control logs pod dash c init container before changing anything.

1.title: Lab 3.1: sidecar log tailer
1.text: Lab three point one: sidecar log tailer. This task is worth six points, and you should plan about seven minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context.

1.title: Lab 3.1: sidecar log tailer, continued
1.text: Lab three point one: sidecar log tailer, continued. In the namespace mc, the Pod weblog (manifest about slash work slash weblog dot yaml ) has one container app that appends lines to slash var slash log slash app slash app dot log on the empty dir volume logs. Add a sidecar container named tailer with the image busy box one dot thirty-six that runs tail dash F slash var slash log slash app slash app dot log and mounts the same volume at the same path, so that kube control logs weblog dash c tailer shows the log lines. A running Pod cannot gain a container, so recreate the Pod and wait until both containers are Running. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

1.title: Lab 3.1: sidecar log tailer, Solution
1.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control dash n mc delete pod weblog the wait flag set to true. cat about slash work slash weblog dot yaml. The manifest comes next, as shown on the screen. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

1.title: Lab 3.1: sidecar log tailer, Solution, continued
1.text: Lab three point one: sidecar log tailer, Solution, continued. Run - name tailer. Then image busy box one dot thirty-six. Then command sh, dash c, tail dash F slash var slash log slash app slash app dot log. Then volume Mounts. Then - name logs, mount Path slash var slash log slash app. Then volumes. Then - name logs. Then empty dir. Then Y. The remaining lines are on the screen.

2.title: Lab 3.2: init container content
2.text: Lab three point two: init container content. This task is worth seven points, and you should plan about seven minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. In the namespace mc, create a Pod named site with one init container content (image busy box one dot thirty-six ) and one container web (image engine X alpine ). The init container must write the text welcome to C K A D to the file index dot html on an empty dir volume named html; the web container mounts that volume at slash usr slash share slash engine X slash html. When the Pod is Ready, requesting it over H T T P must return welcome to C K A D. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 3.2: init container content, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. kube control dash n mc apply dash f -. The manifest comes next, as shown on the screen. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 3.2: init container content, Solution, continued
2.text: Lab three point two: init container content, Solution, continued. Run image engine X alpine. Then volume Mounts. Then - name html, mount Path slash usr slash share slash engine X slash html. Then volumes. Then - name html. Then empty dir. Then Y. Then kube control dash n mc wait the for flag set to condition Ready pod slash site the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds.

2.title: Lab 3.3: init waits for service
2.text: Lab three point three: init waits for service. This task is worth six points, and you should plan about seven minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. In the namespace mc, the Pods of the Deployment web are stuck in Init zero slash one: their init container waits until H T T P colon slash slash backend answers. The Deployment backend is running. Without changing the Deployment web, make the Pods of web start and become Ready (two of two). Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 3.3: init waits for service, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control dash n mc describe pod dash l app web then pipe to grep -A three Init Containers. Then kube control dash n mc logs deploy slash web dash c wait backend the tail flag set to three. Then kube control dash n mc get svc. Then kube control dash n mc expose deployment backend the port flag set to eighty. Then kube control dash n mc rollout status deployment web the timeout flag set to one hundred eighty seconds. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 3.4: shared localhost
2.text: Lab three point four: shared local host. This task is worth five points, and you should plan about six minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. In the namespace mc, create one Pod named pair with two containers: web (image engine X alpine ) and checker (image busy box one dot thirty-six ). The checker must run sh dash c while true do W get dash q dash O slash dev slash null H T T P colon slash slash local host eighty echo ok sleep three done, so its log shows ok as long as it can reach the web container over local host (containers of one Pod share the network). Wait until the Pod is Ready. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 3.4: shared localhost, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. kube control dash n mc apply dash f -. The manifest comes next, as shown on the screen. Then kube control dash n mc wait the for flag set to condition Ready pod slash pair the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds. Then sleep six. Then kube control dash n mc logs pair dash c checker. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 3.5: native sidecar job
2.text: Lab three point five: native sidecar job. This task is worth seven points, and you should plan about eight minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context.

2.title: Lab 3.5: native sidecar job, continued
2.text: Lab three point five: native sidecar job, continued. In the namespace mc, the Job report never completes, because its Pod has a second container tail (a log helper that sleeps forever) next to the main container main. Keep the tail container, but change the Job so that it completes: declare tail as a native sidecar (an init container with restart Policy Always ). The manifest is in about slash work slash report job dot yaml. A Job's Pod template cannot be edited, so delete the Job and create it again from the corrected file; wait until the Job is complete. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 3.5: native sidecar job, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control dash n mc delete job report the wait flag set to true. cat about slash work slash report job dot yaml. The manifest comes next, as shown on the screen. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 3.5: native sidecar job, Solution, continued
2.text: Lab three point five: native sidecar job, Solution, continued. Run image busy box one dot thirty-six. Then command sleep, three thousand six hundred. Then restart Policy Always. Then containers. Then - name main. Then image busy box one dot thirty-six. Then command sh, dash c, echo report finished. Then Y. Then kube control apply dash f about slash work slash report job dot yaml. The remaining lines are on the screen.

2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What do all containers of one Pod share? Answer: The network (one I P address and local host ) and the volumes they mount. Question two. When do init containers run? Answer: One after another, to completion, before the main containers start. Question three. What does Init zero slash one mean? Answer: The first of the Pod's one init containers has not finished yet.

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. How do you declare a native sidecar? Answer: As an init container with restart Policy Always. Question five. Why does a normal sidecar stop a Job from completing, and how does a native sidecar fix it? Answer: A normal container that never exits keeps the Pod running; a native sidecar is stopped after the main containers finish. Question six. Which flag reads the log of one container in a multi-container Pod? Answer: dash c container (for example kube control logs weblog dash c tailer ).

2.title: Recall Check 3
2.text: Recall check three. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question seven. Which pattern lets the main container reach a database through a local proxy? Answer: The ambassador pattern. Question eight. Can you add a container to a running Pod? Answer: No; recreate the Pod (or edit the Deployment).

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Shared: network ( local host ) and mounted volumes, not the image file system. Init container: init containers, runs to completion first; status Init n slash m; log with dash c. Sidecar: extra container in containers, shares an empty dir. Native sidecar: init container with restart Policy Always; Jobs can complete. Ambassador or adapter: proxy to the outside or converts output; ordinary containers. Add a container: recreate the Pod: replace the force flag. Which container: logs dash c, exec dash c, the all containers flag.
